title: Removable, Jump and Infinite Discontinuities
quickIdea: A removable discontinuity is a hole, a jump has two different finite one-sided limits, and an infinite discontinuity blows up to +-infinity.
remember: Removable: the two-sided limit exists but differs from f(a), or f(a) is undefined. Repairing it means redefining the single value f(a).
Jump: both one-sided limits exist and are finite, but they differ. No single value at a can repair it.
Infinite: at least one one-sided limit is +-infinity or -infinity, as with 1/x at 0 or 1/(x^3 - 27) at 3.
Oscillatory: neither one-sided limit exists even in the extended sense, as with sin(1/x) at 0.
Read the type off the numbers, not off the picture: compute LHL and RHL first and the classification follows.
A function discontinuous at a point can still be continuous everywhere else; a question may ask for the count of discontinuities.

example.prompt: Classify the discontinuities at x = 3 of the three failing options of GATE CSE 2013 Q.22.
example.work: Option (B): f(3) = 4 but 8 - x -> 5 from both sides, so the limit exists and differs from the value - removable. Option (C): x + 3 -> 6 from the left and x - 4 -> -1 from the right, both finite and different - jump. Option (D): 1/(x^3 - 27) -> -infinity from the left and +infinity from the right, and f(3) is undefined - infinite.
example.answer: Removable for (B), jump for (C), infinite for (D). Only (A) is continuous.

gateAngle: The classification is what makes 2013 Q.22 quick: three options fail in three different ways, and naming the type is faster than evaluating all four. The classification is also the reasoning inside a continuity question: once the one-sided limits are known, the verdict follows without further work.

variations.label: ORIGINAL PYQ-STYLE QUESTION
variations.question: Classify the discontinuity of g(x) = |x|/x at x = 0.
variations.answer: A jump. LHL = -1 and RHL = 1; both are finite and they differ, so no value at 0 could make g continuous.
variations.why: The smallest jump there is. Comparing it with the removable case (where the one-sided limits agree) is the whole distinction.

variations.label: CONCEPTUAL PRACTICE QUESTION
variations.question: Why can a removable discontinuity be repaired but a jump cannot?
variations.answer: Because repairing means choosing one value for f(a), and that value must equal the two-sided limit. A removable discontinuity has a two-sided limit, so one value works; a jump has no two-sided limit, so no single value can equal it.
variations.why: The repair test is exactly 'does the two-sided limit exist'. It is also why the terminology matters in a question that asks which discontinuity is removable.

trap.what: Calling any break in the graph 'removable', or assuming that a function which fails to be continuous must fail at only one point.
trap.why: Removable means specifically that the two-sided limit exists. A jump and an infinite discontinuity have no two-sided limit at all, and functions can be discontinuous at infinitely many points while being continuous elsewhere.
trap.counterexample: f(x) = 1/(x^3 - 27) at x = 3 has one-sided limits -infinity and +infinity, so no two-sided limit exists and the break is not removable. And a function can be discontinuous at more than one point: f(x) = 0 at rational x and 1 at irrational x is discontinuous at every real number.

check.question: f(x) = x + 1 for x < 2, f(x) = x + 3 for x > 2, f(2) = 3. What type of discontinuity is at x = 2?
check.explanation: LHL = 3 and RHL = 5: both finite and different, so the two-sided limit does not exist and the break cannot be repaired by redefining f(2).
